claims.claim: Kay says the idea of exile lets a novelist underscore elements of the society being evoked by asking why people are exiled, what it means for them and for those left behind.
claims.quote: underscore elements of the society being evoked
claims.page: body, on exile as a technique

claims.claim: Kay says he does not write novels inspired by history to offer easy parallels to our own time, because that can feel lazy or glib or both.
claims.quote: That can feel lazy, or glib, or both

claims.claim: Kay praises Penelope Fitzgerald's short novels for achieving so much with such small strokes that they frequently feel miraculous.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, '6 Books I Love', cbc.ca
claims.quote: achieve so much with such small strokes

claims.feature: other: not talking down to the reader
claims.claim: Kay praises Dorothy Dunnett for flatly refusing to talk down to her readers, making demands and rewarding them.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, '6 Books I Love', cbc.ca
claims.quote: flatly refuses to talk down to her readers

claims.feature: other: quarter turn to the fantastic
claims.claim: Kay tells The Guardian he steeps himself in a period and then twists it just a little to give himself ethical and creative space.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, quoted by Alison Flood, The Guardian
claims.quote: I steep myself in a period and then I twist it
claims.page: later in the article, on El Cid

claims.feature: other: quarter turn to the fantastic

claims.quote: history with a quarter-turn to the fantastic

claims.claim: Kay says he has been calling the current practice an epidemic of co-opting real lives, while declining to criticise writers who do it.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, quoted by Alison Flood, The Guardian
claims.quote: an epidemic of co-opting real lives

claims.feature: other: competing versions of one story
claims.claim: Kay says Children of Earth and Sky has several scenes in which one conversation is described by more than one of the people in it, and that when he switches point of view the conversation is not the same.

claims.quote: as described by more than one of the people in the conversation

claims.feature: other: competing versions of one story

claims.quote: another character’s point of view, the conversation isn’t the same
claims.page: answer on multiple points of view

claims.claim: Kay says you can have a forgotten emperor while the chronicler of the reign is remembered, citing Ezra Pound on Homer and Troy.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, interviewed by Christine Fischer Guy, LARB
claims.quote: a forgotten emperor and the chronicler of the reign is remembered
claims.page: answer on art enduring after empires

claims.feature: other: seam between invention and record must not show
claims.claim: Kay says that if a reader can pick out what is made up and what is real, the storytelling has been botched.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, interviewed by Christine Fischer Guy, LARB
claims.quote: pick out what’s made up and what’s real, you’ve botched your storytelling
claims.page: answer on interrogating a version of the past

claims.feature: other: a signal that the world is not ours
claims.claim: Kay says he has used two moons in several books as a signal, and that the two moons say we are not here.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, interviewed by Christine Fischer Guy, LARB
claims.quote: The two moons say, We’re not here
claims.page: answer on setting the rules of engagement

claims.claim: Kay says that at most times and places in history the only people you could rely upon were your kin, and that those cut off from kinship bonds were in radical danger.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, interviewed by Christine Fischer Guy, LARB
claims.quote: the only people you could rely upon were your kin

claims.claim: Kay says the past is for him staggeringly alien and that writers about the past should acknowledge and work with that.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, interviewed by Christine Fischer Guy, LARB

claims.claim: Kay says the fantastic lets him make the world be as his characters believe it to be, and that the reader then accepts it without any sense that the worldview is quaint.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, interviewed by Christine Fischer Guy, LARB
claims.quote: without any sense that the worldview is quaint
claims.page: closing answers on how the fantastic serves him
